name: Paired conjunctions: both … and, either … or, neither … nor
subtitle: These words come in pairs: both … and, either … or, neither … nor, not only … but also. If you use the first part, you need the second. She speaks both French and Spanish. I like neither tea nor coffee.

concept.exampleHtml: He has not only a good job, but also a lovely flat. · She speaks both French and Spanish.

qa.html: both … and means two things are true, and they are equal. She speaks both French and Spanish. The hotel is both cheap and clean. The verb is plural: Both Amira and Diego are late.
not only … but also means two things are true, but the second one is the surprise. He is not only clever but also very kind. She not only sings but also plays the guitar.
either … or means one of two, not both. We can go either today or tomorrow. You can pay either by card or in cash.
neither … nor means not the first and not the second. It is already negative, so do not add not or don't: I like neither tea nor coffee. The room is neither big nor bright.

Put the pair directly before the two things you compare. They must have the same form (two nouns, two adjectives, two verbs, two phrases). She is both a teacher and a writer. He can either stay or go. With either … or, neither … nor and not only … but also, the verb agrees with the nearer subject: Neither Tom nor his sisters are coming. Either his sisters or Tom is coming.

Typical mistakes: ✗ I don't like neither tea nor coffee. → ✓ I like neither tea nor coffee. (neither is already negative) · ✗ She speaks both French or Spanish. → ✓ She speaks both French and Spanish. (the pair is both … and) · ✗ She is both a nurse and works at night. → ✓ She is both a nurse and a student. (same form after both and and)

concept.noteHtml: Neither … nor sounds formal in speech. People often say I don't like tea or coffee or I like neither of them. For more negative words see negative words and negation. Not only can start a sentence, but then the word order changes: Not only did he forget, but he also lied. You will see this in formal writing, so you only need to recognise it. To link a fact and its opposite, see contrast.

hoeren.instruction: Listen and choose the pair of words you hear. You can listen twice.

items.text: I like neither tea nor coffee.
We can go either by bus or by train.
She speaks both French and Spanish.
He is not only clever but also hardworking.
Neither Tom nor his sisters are coming.
The room is neither big nor bright.

rounds.label: 1 · not only … but also
rounds.instruction: You hear two short sentences. Join them with not only … but also.

example.prompt: He has a good job. He has a lovely flat.
example.answer: He has not only a good job but also a lovely flat.

items.prompt: She is clever. She is hard-working.
items.answer: She is not only clever but also hard-working.

items.prompt: The room is big. The room is bright.
items.answer: The room is not only big but also bright.

items.prompt: He speaks French. He speaks Italian.
items.answer: He speaks not only French but also Italian.

items.prompt: I like tea. I like coffee.
items.answer: I like not only tea but also coffee.

items.prompt: The film was long. The film was boring.
items.answer: The film was not only long but also boring.

items.prompt: She sings. She plays the guitar.
items.answer: She not only sings but also plays the guitar.

rounds.label: 2 · neither … nor
rounds.instruction: Now both are not true. Say it with neither … nor, without don't or not.

example.prompt: I don't drink coffee. I don't drink tea.
example.answer: I drink neither coffee nor tea.

items.prompt: He doesn't eat meat. He doesn't eat fish.
items.answer: He eats neither meat nor fish.

items.prompt: She hasn't got a car. She hasn't got a bike.
items.answer: She has neither a car nor a bike.

items.prompt: I have no time. I have no money.
items.answer: I have neither time nor money.

items.prompt: The room has no window. It has no balcony.
items.answer: The room has neither a window nor a balcony.

items.prompt: He doesn't speak Spanish. He doesn't speak Italian.
items.answer: He speaks neither Spanish nor Italian.

items.prompt: We don't know the way. We don't know the town.
items.answer: We know neither the way nor the town.

exercises.title: Gap text: A weekend in Wales.
exercises.hint: Each gap is one part of a pair. The other part is in the sentence and tells you which one is missing.

segments.text: Amira and Diego are planning a weekend in Wales. Amira likes
cities and the countryside, but this time she wants some quiet. Diego is
a good cook but also a careful driver. They want to go
to the sea or to a lake. In August the sea is
cheap nor quiet, so they choose the lake. They will take either a tent
a small caravan. The campsite has both a kitchen
a bathroom. The lake is not only beautiful
warm enough for swimming. The village shop sells neither bread
milk, so they bring their own.

exercises.title: Match the two halves.
exercises.hint: The first part tells you which second part must follow.

pairs.q: You can pay either by card

exercises.title: Pair or verb? Complete the sentences.
exercises.hint: Look at the other half of the pair. For the verb, look at the nearer subject.

items.prompt: She speaks both French ___ Spanish.
We can have either soup ___ salad.
I like neither tea ___ coffee.
He is ___ clever but also funny.
items.why: But also belongs to not only.

items.prompt: I like ___ tea nor coffee.
Neither Tom nor his sisters ___ coming.
items.why: The nearer subject (his sisters) is plural.

items.prompt: Either my parents or my brother ___ going to pick me up.
items.why: The nearer subject (my brother) is singular.

items.prompt: Both Amira and Diego ___ late.
items.why: Both … and joins two people, so the verb is plural.
